Basic BGP Troubleshooting on Junos

A practical playbook for diagnosing neighbor state, route advertisement/reception, path selection, and safe use of traceoptions.

In this lesson: show bgp summary, show route advertising-protocol, show route receive-protocol
Coming up: traceoptions setup, file viewing, and clean-up best practices
Why this matters

BGP misconfigurations cause traffic loss and routing instability. A repeatable troubleshooting order reduces outages and speeds recovery in production networks.

Visual Concept
Session → Route Exchange → Path Selection
Session
show bgp summary, show bgp neighbor — state, timers, capabilities
Routes
advertising-protocol & receive-protocol to compare sent and received routes
Best Path

Explore Key Topics

Focus on three repeatable checks to find the cause quickly and safely.

Neighbor states: what each TCP/FSM state usually means
Route exchange checks: advertising vs receive-protocol
Traceoptions: how to capture then remove debug logs

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of these exercises you will reliably identify and fix common BGP problems using the Junos CLI. First, you will learn to recognize neighbor session failures and map them to either TCP connectivity or BGP parameter mismatches. Second, you will practice using advertising and receive-protocol commands to confirm exactly what routes are sent and what arrives before policies apply. Third, you will apply troubleshooting techniques to correct route advertisement and reception failures, including checking network statements, family configuration, and import/export policies. Fourth, you will know when to enable traceoptions for message-level debugging and how to safely remove them. Each objective is tied to a competency milestone so you can verify that you performed the right commands and interpreted outputs correctly. For example, after learning the neighbor checks you should be able to run show bgp summary and, given its state, list the most likely causes and the next non-disruptive command to run. These skills matter because BGP issues directly affect reachability and traffic engineering, and the right command order minimizes risk to production routing.

Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Learning Objectives

Learning Objectives

Master checks and Junos commands to troubleshoot BGP sessions, routes, and path selection.

Bloom: Learn → Understand → Apply → Master
01
Identify common BGP issues

Detect neighbor down, routes not advertised or received, and unexpected path selection using stateful observation. Verified competency milestone: explain causes from a show bgp summary output.

VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE
02
Use Junos CLI for diagnosis

VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE

Check network statements, family inet unicast, export/import policies, and next-hop reachability to restore expected route exchange. Milestone: demonstrate restoring advertisements in a lab scenario.

Use BGP traceoptions safely

Enable targeted traceoptions, collect logs, then deactivate traces to avoid resource issues. Milestone: capture and interpret a trace of a session open exchange.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Milestones
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives screen focuses on practical verification and avoidance of common mistakes. For neighbor session failures you will be expected to run show bgp summary and then one or two follow-up read-only commands such as ping or show route to confirm IP reachability. For route advertisement issues you will show the advertising-protocol output and inspect export policies and family settings before changing configuration. When routes are not received, you must demonstrate the difference between receive-protocol and protocol routes, proving whether the peer sent the route or your import policy blocked it. For path selection issues you will compare attributes in show route detail and identify whether LOCAL_PREF, AS_PATH, or MED is causing the choice. Finally, when enabling traceoptions you will set a small file size and specific flags, observe log output, then deactivate traces. Each milestone is deliberately observable: the instructor or operator should be able to run the same show commands and confirm the same conclusions you reached. This makes troubleshooting repeatable and auditable in production.

Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Verification Milestones
Neighbor Failure Milestone
From show bgp summary, identify the FSM state and list two non-disruptive follow-ups that confirm reachability or parameter mismatch.
Advertisement Milestone
Use show route advertising-protocol and show route <prefix> to prove the prefix exists and is being offered to a peer.
Reception Milestone
Compare receive-protocol and protocol outputs to prove whether an import policy or next-hop reachability removed a received route.
Path Selection Milestone
Show route <prefix> detail and explain which attribute decided the best path and why a policy may have changed it.
Traceoptions Milestone
Enable a targeted trace with limited file size and flags, reproduce the event, capture logs, then deactivate traces and show the file output with show log.
Key Takeaway

Verification requires repeatable evidence: prefer show commands, document outputs, and avoid destructive clears until necessary.

screens.title: Diagnosing Neighbor State
screens.narratorSegment: The first and simplest BGP check is neighbor state. Run show bgp summary to see each peer and its Finite State Machine state. When you see Established, you can move on to route checks. However, if the state is Active or Connect it almost always indicates a TCP connectivity problem. Active means the router is still trying to connect; Connect means the TCP handshake has not completed. For these states check IP reachability using ping, verify interface status with show interfaces terse, and inspect the local routing table with show route. For iBGP using loopbacks ensure the local-address configured for the peer is reachable and correct. Also confirm that TCP port 179 is not blocked by an ACL or firewall. A common misconception is to assume BGP alone will establish transport; in fact the underlying IP connectivity and source IP selection determine whether the TCP session can be formed. Concrete example: you see a peer stuck in Active. You ping the neighbor IP, it fails; show interfaces reveals the interface to the neighbor is administratively down. Fixing the interface restores reachability and allows the session to progress to Established. Takeaway: neighbor state tells you whether to look at transport or BGP parameters next.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Diagnosing Neighbor State
Core Concept

Interpret FSM states from show bgp summary

Use the neighbor state to decide whether to check transport or BGP parameters. Active/Connect usually means TCP problems; OpenSent/OpenConfirm suggests parameter mismatch.

  • IP reachability: run ping to the neighbor IP to confirm basic transport.
  • Interface check: show interfaces terse to find administratively down or wrong IP.
  • Routing to neighbor: show route <neighbor-ip-address> ensures a route exists for TCP sessions over loopbacks.
Common mistake
Assuming BGP will form a session without verifying the underlying IP path and the source address used for TCP.
Key Takeaway

Neighbor FSM states point you to either TCP/infrastructure issues or BGP parameter mismatches. Validate reachability first.

Terminal Demo
show bgp summary Neighbor AS Up/Down State 10.0.0.2 65002 never Active # Follow-ups ping 10.0.0.2 show interfaces terse show route 10.0.0.2
Concrete example
Peer stuck in Active. Ping fails. show interfaces terse reveals interface to neighbor is down. Bring interface up and session progresses to Established.

screens.title: TCP Connectivity Checks
screens.narratorSegment: When a neighbor session fails at the transport layer, a short process reduces noise and finds the fault quickly. Start with ping to confirm IP reachability to the neighbor IP. If ping fails, inspect interface status with show interfaces terse and validate the IP address configuration. Next, check the routing table using show route to ensure your router has a route to that IP. For iBGP with loopback peers, verify the configured local-address is reachable and matches the loopback address used during the TCP handshake. Also confirm that TCP port 179 is permitted end-to-end; firewalls or ACLs that block this port will prevent session establishment. A common troubleshooting misstep is to only check the immediate link and forget intermediate filters or firewall devices along the path. Practical example: ping succeeds but the session still fails; show route indicates asymmetric return path, and an ACL on a transit device drops TCP 179. Fix the ACL and the session establishes. Always document the checks you run so changes are auditable and reversible. TCP Connectivity Checks means ping → interfaces → route → source-address → confirm tcp 179 is allowed along the path.. In practical terms, pinpoint ip reachability, source address, and port 179 barriers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › TCP Connectivity Checks
Process Flow

A short checklist for TCP reachability

  1. ping <neighbor-ip-address> to confirm basic connectivity.
  2. show interfaces terse to check link and IP configuration.
  3. show route <neighbor-ip-address> to verify routing to the peer.
  4. For loopback peering, validate local-address is reachable from the peer.
  5. Confirm TCP port 179 is allowed by any ACLs or firewalls in path.
Misconception
A successful ping does not guarantee TCP 179 is permitted. Always test or verify port filtering separately.
Terminal Demo
ping 10.0.0.2
show interfaces terse
show route 10.0.0.2
# For loopback peer
show route 192.0.2.2
Scenario
Ping succeeds but TCP 179 is blocked by an ACL on a transit device. The session stays in Connect. Fix the ACL and re-verify the session advances to Established.

screens.title: OpenSent / OpenConfirm Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: If your neighbor session stalls in OpenSent or OpenConfirm the most likely cause is a mismatch in BGP parameters exchanged in the Open messages. The immediate items to check are AS numbers, any configured authentication, BGP version mismatches on very old equipment, and hold timers. For eBGP specifically, a common mistake is configuring the wrong peer-as on one side, or swapping AS numbers. The show bgp neighbor command is your best next step because it reveals the FSM state, last errors, and capability negotiation. If authentication is configured, verify keys match on both routers. Hold time mismatches rarely prevent establishment but can cause instability if one side enforces a stricter timer. Compare this with an Active/Connect situation: Active/Connect points to transport issues; OpenSent/OpenConfirm points to protocol parameter disagreements. Concrete example: an OpenConfirm state showing a Notification about unsupported capability directs you to capability or version mismatches. After correcting the peer-as or the authentication keys, the session should progress to Established. Always re-run show bgp neighbor to confirm the last error changed and the session moved forward. OpenSent / OpenConfirm Troubleshooting means opensent/openconfirm usually indicates as mismatch, auth mismatch, or capability differences—use show bgp neighbor to inspect.. In practical terms, parameter mismatches to check in open messages. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › OpenSent / OpenConfirm
Comparison

Parameter mismatches vs transport issues

Check AS numbers: Ensure peer-as matches the neighbor's configured autonomous-system.
Authentication: If MD5 or other auth is in use, keys must match exactly.
Capabilities: Some vendors or old devices may not support negotiated capabilities; check last errors.
Hold time: Mismatched timers can cause negotiation or session flaps if misaligned.
Command to run
show bgp neighbor 10.0.0.2
Terminal Output Example
Neighbor: 10.0.0.2, Peer AS: 65002
  State: OpenConfirm
  Last error: Notification received - Unsupported Capability
Concrete fix
Find the capability mismatch or wrong peer-as, correct the configuration, then re-check the neighbor state until it shows Established.

screens.title: Routes Not Advertised — Diagnosis
screens.narratorSegment: When a peer reports they are not receiving routes you expect, start by proving what your router is advertising. The primary command is show route advertising-protocol bgp. This output shows exactly which routes your router is sending to that neighbor. If a prefix is missing from advertising-protocol, investigate whether the prefix exists in inet.0 and whether your configuration intends to advertise it. Use show route to confirm the prefix exists as an exact match. If you rely on network statements, remember the advertised route must be present in the routing table to be sent. Next, inspect your export policy: export rules may filter or transform routes so they are not advertised. Use show policy policy-statement and test policy to simulate how the policy treats a route. Also confirm your BGP group is configured for the appropriate address family, for example family inet unicast. A common mistake is assuming the presence of a network statement automatically advertises a prefix; the prefix must be in the routing table and permitted by export policy and family settings. The takeaway: show route advertising-protocol is the single best read-only command to confirm what you send.

keyIdea.text: Use show route advertising-protocol to confirm which prefixes are actually being offered to a peer.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Routes Not Advertised
Definition

Prove what you are sending

show route advertising-protocol bgp <neighbor-ip> reveals the routes your router offers. If a route is missing, verify route existence, export policy, and address-family configuration.

  • Confirm prefix exists: show route <prefix>
  • Test export policy: test policy <policy-name> <route-to-test>
  • Check family: ensure family inet unicast is set for the BGP group.
Common mistake
Assuming a network statement advertises a prefix even if the route is absent from inet.0 or blocked by export policy.
Terminal Demo
show route advertising-protocol bgp 10.0.0.2
# If 192.168.20.0/24 not listed
show route 192.168.20.0/24
show policy policy-statement EXPORT-TO-ISP
test policy EXPORT-TO-ISP 192.168.20.0/24
Concrete fix
If route missing from inet.0, ensure network statement or IGP installs it. If export policy denies it, update the policy and re-check advertising-protocol output.

screens.title: Routes Not Received — Diagnosis
screens.narratorSegment: When you expect to receive routes from a peer but don't see them in your routing table, the first step is to determine whether the peer sent the routes. Use show route receive-protocol bgp to list routes received from that neighbor before any import policies. If a route appears here but not in show route protocol bgp, your import policy or next-hop reachability likely removed it. Check import policy definitions with show policy policy-statement and test policy to simulate route handling. For iBGP scenarios, ensure your IGP has a route to the BGP next-hop; otherwise received routes will be invalid and not accepted. Use show route to verify next-hop reachability. Another important cause is AS_PATH loop detection: if the received AS_PATH contains your local AS, the route is discarded. A common misconception is to only look at show route protocol bgp; always compare receive-protocol output with accepted protocol routes to pinpoint whether the issue is on the peer's side or in your own import policy. Example: a prefix shows in receive-protocol but not in protocol output; test policy reveals an import statement denying that prefix. Fixing the import policy allows the route to populate the BGP table.

keyIdea.text: Use receive-protocol to see what was sent, then compare to accepted routes to find where policies or next-hop checks dropped a route.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Routes Not Received
Core Concept

Was the route sent or dropped locally?

show route receive-protocol bgp <neighbor> lists what the peer sent before import policies. Compare that to show route protocol bgp to see what was accepted.

  • If in receive-protocol but not accepted: inspect import policy or next-hop reachability.
  • Check next-hop with show route <next-hop-ip> for iBGP scenarios.
  • Watch for AS_PATH loops: if local AS present, route is discarded.
Terminal Demo
show route receive-protocol bgp 10.0.0.2
show route protocol bgp
show route 192.0.2.1
show policy policy-statement IMPORT-FROM-ISP
test policy IMPORT-FROM-ISP 203.0.113.0/24
Concrete example
Route present in receive-protocol but absent from protocol. test policy shows import policy denies the prefix. Update import policy to accept the prefix and re-check that the BGP table contains the route.

screens.title: Inspecting Path Selection
screens.narratorSegment: When BGP chooses a path you don't expect, the show route detail command is the most useful single step. It lists all received paths for the prefix, their attributes such as AS_PATH, LOCAL_PREF, MED, Origin, and Next-Hop, and which path is selected as Active. Review the BGP best path algorithm sequence—LOCAL_PREF precedes AS_PATH, which precedes MED in many cases—and compare attributes across competing paths. Also examine import/export policies that may have modified attributes, such as setting a higher LOCAL_PREF or prepending to AS_PATH. A common misconception is to assume the shortest AS_PATH always wins; in practice LOCAL_PREF or policy can override that. Concrete example: two ISP links advertise the same prefix. The less preferred link is chosen because its LOCAL_PREF is higher due to a misapplied import policy. Use show route detail to spot the attribute differences, then correct the import policy to adjust LOCAL_PREF for the preferred link. Always re-run show route detail after policy changes to confirm the expected best path is selected. Inspecting Path Selection means use show route <prefix> detail to compare attributes and identify which attribute caused an unexpected selection.. In practical terms, use show route <prefix> detail to compare bgp path attributes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Inspecting Path Selection
Core Concept

Compare path attributes to find the best path reason

Look at LOCAL_PREF, AS_PATH, MED, Origin, and Next-Hop. Policies may alter these attributes and change selection.

LOCAL_PREF: higher is preferred and often set by import policy.
AS_PATH: shorter paths are preferred unless local policy overrides.
MED: lower is preferred when comparing paths from the same neighbor AS.
Pro-tip
When multiple ISPs present differing LOCAL_PREF values, audit import policies on both ISP sessions to ensure expected preferences.

show route 0.0.0.0/0 detail
# Compare attributes among available paths
# If LOCAL_PREF unusual, inspect import policy that sets it
show policy policy-statement IMPORT-ISP-A
show policy policy-statement IMPORT-ISP-B

Two ISP links show different LOCAL_PREF values due to misconfigured import policies. Adjust the import policy for the preferred link to set a higher LOCAL_PREF and re-check the active path.

screens.title: BGP Traceoptions for Deep Debugging
screens.narratorSegment: Traceoptions provide message-level detail about BGP events, including Open, Update, and state transitions. Use them only when show commands do not reveal enough information, and always limit file size and flags to reduce resource impact. The canonical configuration sequence sets a small file, several rotated files, and the flags you need. For example, enabling flags state and open captures FSM transitions and Open message exchanges. After reproducing the problem, view the trace with show log. Traceoptions output helps when you need to know the exact message contents, timers, or notification reasons the router received. Always deactivate traceoptions and commit the change when you finish; leaving traces active can fill disk space and burden the control plane. A common mistake is enabling flag all with a large file size in production and forgetting to turn it off. Concrete example: enable traceoptions for state and open, clear the neighbor so Open messages reappear, and inspect bgp-debug to find a Notification indicating an AS mismatch. Deactivate traceoptions and commit the clean-up. Use traceoptions as a precise tool to gather evidence when show commands are insufficient.

Definition

What traceoptions capture

Traceoptions log BGP message exchanges and FSM transitions in detail. Use flags to focus on state, open, or updates rather than logging everything.

screens.narratorSegment: This practical scenario demonstrates the sequence to diagnose which ISP link traffic prefers when you expect the other to be primary. Process Flow

Stepwise diagnosis for multi-homing

screens.title: Lab Walkthrough: Introduce and Fix Errors
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on walkthrough follows the source activity that introduces two errors and then resolves them. Start on R1 configured to peer with R2 at 10.0.0.2. Step one: intentionally set the wrong peer-as on R1 to 65003 and commit. Observe the session fail with run show bgp summary and run show bgp neighbor 10.0.0.2. The neighbor output will show an Open or Notification indicating AS mismatch. Correct the peer-as to the right value and commit. Verify the session becomes Established. Step two: deactivate family inet unicast on the BGP group and commit. This causes R1 to stop advertising IPv4 unicast routes. On R1 run run show route advertising-protocol bgp 10.0.0.2 and on R2 run run show route receive-protocol bgp 10.0.0.2 to confirm no routes are exchanged. Reactivate family inet unicast on R1 and commit. Finally, as a controlled debug exercise enable traceoptions flags state and open with a small file, clear the neighbor to force Open messages, view show log bgp-debug to see the Open exchange, then deactivate traceoptions and commit. The lab demonstrates a repeatable cycle: introduce, diagnose with show commands, correct, and verify with the same show commands.

Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Lab Walkthrough
Hands-on Activity

Introduce, diagnose, correct, verify

  1. Set wrong peer-as on R1 and commit to simulate Open mismatch.
  2. Run run show bgp summary and run show bgp neighbor to find errors.
  3. Fix peer-as, commit, and verify Established state.
  4. Deactivate family inet unicast on R1 to simulate no advertisement.

Commands (on R1)
edit
set protocols bgp group EBGP_PEER neighbor 10.0.0.2 peer-as 65003
commit
run show bgp summary
run show bgp neighbor 10.0.0.2
set protocols bgp group EBGP_PEER neighbor 10.0.0.2 peer-as 65002
commit
# Simulate advertising issue
deactivate protocols bgp group EBGP_PEER family inet unicast
commit
run show route advertising-protocol bgp 10.0.0.2
# Restore

commit

set protocols bgp traceoptions file bgp-debug size 1m files 2
set protocols bgp traceoptions flag state
set protocols bgp traceoptions flag open
commit

run show log bgp-debug
deactivate protocols bgp traceoptions
commit

screens.title: Safety and Non-Disruptive Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: When troubleshooting BGP in production, safety is paramount. Start with non-disruptive show commands to gather evidence. Avoid immediate clear bgp neighbor commands unless you understand the impact; clearing a BGP session disrupts routes and may trigger widespread reroutes. Use clear only after you have identified the likely cause and when a session reset will not violate change control procedures. Similarly, be cautious with monitor traffic and packet captures because they can tax the router. Document the commands you ran and the outputs observed so that any remediation steps are auditable. If you must apply a change, prefer incremental policy updates or temporary route filters that are easy to revert. After applying a fix, re-run the same show commands you used during diagnosis to demonstrate that the issue is resolved. A practical habit: capture show outputs before and after a change and attach them to incident notes. This preserves a clear timeline and helps colleagues reproduce and learn from your work. Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Safety & Documentation

Non-disruptive troubleshooting habits

  • Always begin with read-only commands (show bgp summary, show route, show policy).
  • Avoid clear bgp unless you know the impact and have authorization.
  • Limit traceoptions size and flags, and deactivate when finished.
  • Document commands and outputs before making configuration changes.
Checklist
Collect show outputs, identify the cause, propose minimal change, apply during maintenance window if needed, verify using the same show commands.
Why it matters

A careful approach reduces the chance of causing wider routing instability and makes incident handling auditable.

screens.title: Assessment Questions and Explanations
screens.narratorSegment: Two assessment questions help cement the diagnostic logic. First, an eBGP session stuck in OpenSent most likely indicates a mismatch in Open parameters such as AS numbers or authentication. The immediate command to inspect is run show bgp neighbor, which shows the FSM, the last error, and capability negotiation details. This helps you pinpoint whether a Notification was received and why. Second, if you configured a network statement for 192.168.20.0/24 but your ISP does not receive it, run run show route 192.168.20.0/24 to verify the exact match exists in inet.0 and run run show route advertising-protocol bgp to confirm whether the prefix is actually being sent. If the route is absent from the routing table or blocked by export policy or missing family inet unicast, the ISP will not receive it. screens.narratorSegment: These are the core commands and principles to remember. First, show bgp summary gives a quick view of neighbor states and is the natural starting point. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we learn a practical, methodical approach to BGP troubleshooting on Junos. You will understand how to identify why a neighbor session is not established, how to verify whether routes are being advertised or received, and why BGP sometimes picks an unexpected path. We focus on safe, read‑only checks first — a discipline that avoids unintentional disruption in production. You will also see how to enable traceoptions for deep debugging and when to turn them off. Along the way we use concrete Junos commands you can run now: show bgp summary, show bgp neighbor, show route advertising-protocol, show route receive-protocol, and show route detail. A short hands‑on workflow walks you through introducing, diagnosing, and fixing a common misconfiguration. Finally, we highlight common misconceptions, such as assuming an established session guarantees advertised routes, or that clearing a session is always safe. After this lesson you will be able to find the likely cause of neighbor failures, confirm what is actually being sent and accepted, and use traceoptions with care to gather message-level evidence. What problem would you check first on a flapping BGP session?

By the end of these exercises you will reliably identify and fix common BGP problems using the Junos CLI. First, you will learn to recognize neighbor session failures and map them to either TCP connectivity or BGP parameter mismatches. Second, you will practice using advertising and receive-protocol commands to confirm exactly what routes are sent and what arrives before policies apply. Third, you will apply troubleshooting techniques to correct route advertisement and reception failures, including checking network statements, family configuration, and import/export policies. Fourth, you will know when to enable traceoptions for message-level debugging and how to safely remove them. Each objective is tied to a competency milestone so you can verify that you performed the right commands and interpreted outputs correctly. For example, after learning the neighbor checks you should be able to run show bgp summary and, given its state, list the most likely causes and the next non-disruptive command to run. These skills matter because BGP issues directly affect reachability and traffic engineering, and the right command order minimizes risk to production routing.

This second objectives screen focuses on practical verification and avoidance of common mistakes. For neighbor session failures you will be expected to run show bgp summary and then one or two follow-up read-only commands such as ping or show route to confirm IP reachability. For route advertisement issues you will show the advertising-protocol output and inspect export policies and family settings before changing configuration. When routes are not received, you must demonstrate the difference between receive-protocol and protocol routes, proving whether the peer sent the route or your import policy blocked it. For path selection issues you will compare attributes in show route detail and identify whether LOCAL_PREF, AS_PATH, or MED is causing the choice. Finally, when enabling traceoptions you will set a small file size and specific flags, observe log output, then deactivate traces. Each milestone is deliberately observable: the instructor or operator should be able to run the same show commands and confirm the same conclusions you reached. This makes troubleshooting repeatable and auditable in production.

The first and simplest BGP check is neighbor state. Run show bgp summary to see each peer and its Finite State Machine state. When you see Established, you can move on to route checks. However, if the state is Active or Connect it almost always indicates a TCP connectivity problem. Active means the router is still trying to connect; Connect means the TCP handshake has not completed. For these states check IP reachability using ping, verify interface status with show interfaces terse, and inspect the local routing table with show route. For iBGP using loopbacks ensure the local-address configured for the peer is reachable and correct. Also confirm that TCP port 179 is not blocked by an ACL or firewall. A common misconception is to assume BGP alone will establish transport; in fact the underlying IP connectivity and source IP selection determine whether the TCP session can be formed. Concrete example: you see a peer stuck in Active. You ping the neighbor IP, it fails; show interfaces reveals the interface to the neighbor is administratively down. Fixing the interface restores reachability and allows the session to progress to Established. Takeaway: neighbor state tells you whether to look at transport or BGP parameters next.

When a neighbor session fails at the transport layer, a short process reduces noise and finds the fault quickly. Start with ping to confirm IP reachability to the neighbor IP. If ping fails, inspect interface status with show interfaces terse and validate the IP address configuration. Next, check the routing table using show route to ensure your router has a route to that IP. For iBGP with loopback peers, verify the configured local-address is reachable and matches the loopback address used during the TCP handshake. Also confirm that TCP port 179 is permitted end-to-end; firewalls or ACLs that block this port will prevent session establishment. A common troubleshooting misstep is to only check the immediate link and forget intermediate filters or firewall devices along the path. Practical example: ping succeeds but the session still fails; show route indicates asymmetric return path, and an ACL on a transit device drops TCP 179. Fix the ACL and the session establishes. Always document the checks you run so changes are auditable and reversible. TCP Connectivity Checks means ping → interfaces → route → source-address → confirm tcp 179 is allowed along the path.. In practical terms, pinpoint ip reachability, source address, and port 179 barriers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

If your neighbor session stalls in OpenSent or OpenConfirm the most likely cause is a mismatch in BGP parameters exchanged in the Open messages. The immediate items to check are AS numbers, any configured authentication, BGP version mismatches on very old equipment, and hold timers. For eBGP specifically, a common mistake is configuring the wrong peer-as on one side, or swapping AS numbers. The show bgp neighbor command is your best next step because it reveals the FSM state, last errors, and capability negotiation. If authentication is configured, verify keys match on both routers. Hold time mismatches rarely prevent establishment but can cause instability if one side enforces a stricter timer. Compare this with an Active/Connect situation: Active/Connect points to transport issues; OpenSent/OpenConfirm points to protocol parameter disagreements. Concrete example: an OpenConfirm state showing a Notification about unsupported capability directs you to capability or version mismatches. After correcting the peer-as or the authentication keys, the session should progress to Established. Always re-run show bgp neighbor to confirm the last error changed and the session moved forward. OpenSent / OpenConfirm Troubleshooting means opensent/openconfirm usually indicates as mismatch, auth mismatch, or capability differences—use show bgp neighbor to inspect.. In practical terms, parameter mismatches to check in open messages. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When a peer reports they are not receiving routes you expect, start by proving what your router is advertising. The primary command is show route advertising-protocol bgp. This output shows exactly which routes your router is sending to that neighbor. If a prefix is missing from advertising-protocol, investigate whether the prefix exists in inet.0 and whether your configuration intends to advertise it. Use show route to confirm the prefix exists as an exact match. If you rely on network statements, remember the advertised route must be present in the routing table to be sent. Next, inspect your export policy: export rules may filter or transform routes so they are not advertised. Use show policy policy-statement and test policy to simulate how the policy treats a route. Also confirm your BGP group is configured for the appropriate address family, for example family inet unicast. A common mistake is assuming the presence of a network statement automatically advertises a prefix; the prefix must be in the routing table and permitted by export policy and family settings. The takeaway: show route advertising-protocol is the single best read-only command to confirm what you send.

When you expect to receive routes from a peer but don't see them in your routing table, the first step is to determine whether the peer sent the routes. Use show route receive-protocol bgp to list routes received from that neighbor before any import policies. If a route appears here but not in show route protocol bgp, your import policy or next-hop reachability likely removed it. Check import policy definitions with show policy policy-statement and test policy to simulate route handling. For iBGP scenarios, ensure your IGP has a route to the BGP next-hop; otherwise received routes will be invalid and not accepted. Use show route to verify next-hop reachability. Another important cause is AS_PATH loop detection: if the received AS_PATH contains your local AS, the route is discarded. A common misconception is to only look at show route protocol bgp; always compare receive-protocol output with accepted protocol routes to pinpoint whether the issue is on the peer's side or in your own import policy. Example: a prefix shows in receive-protocol but not in protocol output; test policy reveals an import statement denying that prefix. Fixing the import policy allows the route to populate the BGP table.

When BGP chooses a path you don't expect, the show route detail command is the most useful single step. It lists all received paths for the prefix, their attributes such as AS_PATH, LOCAL_PREF, MED, Origin, and Next-Hop, and which path is selected as Active. Review the BGP best path algorithm sequence—LOCAL_PREF precedes AS_PATH, which precedes MED in many cases—and compare attributes across competing paths. Also examine import/export policies that may have modified attributes, such as setting a higher LOCAL_PREF or prepending to AS_PATH. A common misconception is to assume the shortest AS_PATH always wins; in practice LOCAL_PREF or policy can override that. Concrete example: two ISP links advertise the same prefix. The less preferred link is chosen because its LOCAL_PREF is higher due to a misapplied import policy. Use show route detail to spot the attribute differences, then correct the import policy to adjust LOCAL_PREF for the preferred link. Always re-run show route detail after policy changes to confirm the expected best path is selected. Inspecting Path Selection means use show route <prefix> detail to compare attributes and identify which attribute caused an unexpected selection.. Traceoptions provide message-level detail about BGP events, including Open, Update, and state transitions. Use them only when show commands do not reveal enough information, and always limit file size and flags to reduce resource impact. The canonical configuration sequence sets a small file, several rotated files, and the flags you need. For example, enabling flags state and open captures FSM transitions and Open message exchanges. After reproducing the problem, view the trace with show log. Traceoptions output helps when you need to know the exact message contents, timers, or notification reasons the router received. Always deactivate traceoptions and commit the change when you finish; leaving traces active can fill disk space and burden the control plane. A common mistake is enabling flag all with a large file size in production and forgetting to turn it off. Concrete example: enable traceoptions for state and open, clear the neighbor so Open messages reappear, and inspect bgp-debug to find a Notification indicating an AS mismatch. Deactivate traceoptions and commit the clean-up. Use traceoptions as a precise tool to gather evidence when show commands are insufficient.

This practical scenario demonstrates the sequence to diagnose which ISP link traffic prefers when you expect the other to be primary. First, verify both BGP sessions are Established with show bgp summary. Next, use show route receive-protocol bgp for each ISP to confirm they advertise the same prefixes. Then run show route detail to examine path attributes for both learned routes, focusing on LOCAL_PREF, AS_PATH, and MED. A common cause of wrong egress is an import policy that unintentionally sets a higher LOCAL_PREF for the less-preferred link. Check import policies for each ISP and test them with test policy. If next-hop differences matter, validate next-hop reachability. After you identify the attribute causing the selection, adjust the import policy—typically setting a higher LOCAL_PREF on routes learned from the preferred ISP—and recheck the selected path with show route detail. Important: make only non-disruptive policy changes first and confirm results in show outputs before committing any clears. This hands-on walkthrough follows the source activity that introduces two errors and then resolves them. Start on R1 configured to peer with R2 at 10.0.0.2. Step one: intentionally set the wrong peer-as on R1 to 65003 and commit. Observe the session fail with run show bgp summary and run show bgp neighbor 10.0.0.2. The neighbor output will show an Open or Notification indicating AS mismatch. Correct the peer-as to the right value and commit. Verify the session becomes Established. Step two: deactivate family inet unicast on the BGP group and commit. This causes R1 to stop advertising IPv4 unicast routes. On R1 run run show route advertising-protocol bgp 10.0.0.2 and on R2 run run show route receive-protocol bgp 10.0.0.2 to confirm no routes are exchanged. When troubleshooting BGP in production, safety is paramount. Start with non-disruptive show commands to gather evidence. Avoid immediate clear bgp neighbor commands unless you understand the impact; clearing a BGP session disrupts routes and may trigger widespread reroutes. Use clear only after you have identified the likely cause and when a session reset will not violate change control procedures. Similarly, be cautious with monitor traffic and packet captures because they can tax the router. Document the commands you ran and the outputs observed so that any remediation steps are auditable. If you must apply a change, prefer incremental policy updates or temporary route filters that are easy to revert. After applying a fix, re-run the same show commands you used during diagnosis to demonstrate that the issue is resolved. A practical habit: capture show outputs before and after a change and attach them to incident notes. This preserves a clear timeline and helps colleagues reproduce and learn from your work. Two assessment questions help cement the diagnostic logic. First, an eBGP session stuck in OpenSent most likely indicates a mismatch in Open parameters such as AS numbers or authentication. The immediate command to inspect is run show bgp neighbor, which shows the FSM, the last error, and capability negotiation details. This helps you pinpoint whether a Notification was received and why. Second, if you configured a network statement for 192.168.20.0/24 but your ISP does not receive it, run run show route 192.168.20.0/24 to verify the exact match exists in inet.0 and run run show route advertising-protocol bgp to confirm whether the prefix is actually being sent. These are the core commands and principles to remember. First, show bgp summary gives a quick view of neighbor states and is the natural starting point. Second, show route advertising-protocol bgp proves what you are actually sending; use it whenever a peer says they are not receiving a prefix. Third, show route receive-protocol bgp shows what the peer sent before import policies, allowing you to differentiate peer-side problems from local policy denial. Finally, show route detail is indispensable for path selection analysis, letting you compare LOCAL_PREF, AS_PATH, MED, and next-hop to determine why a path was selected. Pair these read-only commands with careful policy checks and selective use of traceoptions for detailed message captures. If you keep this small set of commands in your toolbox and follow the non-disruptive workflow, you will be able to diagnose and resolve most basic BGP issues on Junos reliably.

Keep three practical reminders in mind. First, always begin with show commands and gather evidence before making changes. Second, use advertising-protocol and receive-protocol commands to separate peer-side issues from your local policy or routing problems. Third, use traceoptions sparingly with controlled file sizes and flags, then deactivate them after you capture the necessary logs. Practicing this sequence in a lab helps you move quickly and safely in production. These reminders reduce the time to resolution and lower the risk of causing broader routing disruption when you remediate BGP issues.
